Certain it is, that the condition wherein these are has a right the tenderest compassion.
column9:
1. #46 The Wilderness State (wesley-046-c0004): «It properly consists in the loss of that faith which God once wrought in their heart. They that are in the wilderness, have not now that divine "evidence," that satisfactory conviction "of things not seen," which they once enjoyed.» Reason: Defines the wilderness state: loss of the clear faith and sense of God the believer once had.
2. #46 The Wilderness State (wesley-046-c0011): «In consequence of the loss of faith and love, follows, Thirdly, loss of joy in the Holy Ghost. For if the loving consciousness of pardon be no more, the joy resulting therefrom cannot remain.» Reason: Explains why the former joy has gone: it flowed from a faith and witness that have weakened.
3. #46 The Wilderness State (wesley-046-c0013): «That sweet tranquillity of mind, that composure of spirit, is gone. Painful doubt returns; doubt, whether we ever did, and perhaps whether we ever shall, believe.» Reason: Describes the lost peace and the doubts about whether one ever truly believed, a symptom the asker may feel.
4. #46 The Wilderness State (wesley-046-c0019): «Therefore he never deserts us, as some speak; it is we only that desert him. (I.) 2. The most usual cause of inward darkness is sin, of one kind or another.» Reason: Answers 'what happened': God does not arbitrarily withdraw; darkness most often comes from sin.
5. #46 The Wilderness State (wesley-046-c0024): «If therefore we are negligent of this, if we suffer business, company, or any avocation whatever, to prevent these secret exercises of the soul» Reason: Names neglect of private prayer as a common cause of the soul's life gradually dying away.
6. #46 The Wilderness State (wesley-046-c0032): «And if we will not hear his warning voice, and return to him with our whole soul, we continue to grieve him with our idols, and running after other gods, we shall soon be cold, barren, and dry» Reason: Explains how desiring things other than God leaves a believer cold, barren and dry.
7. #46 The Wilderness State (wesley-046-c0034): «Let us only be careless or "faint in our mind," let us be easy and indolent, and our natural darkness will soon return, and overspread our soul.» Reason: Spiritual sloth alone, without gross sin, is enough to darken the soul; a likely cause of drift.
8. #46 The Wilderness State (wesley-046-c0043): «Now, when so various assaults are made at once, and perhaps with the utmost violence, it is not strange if it should occasion, not only heaviness, but even darkness in a weak believer» Reason: Shows that unexpected temptations after a calm season can plunge a believer into darkness.
9. #46 The Wilderness State (wesley-046-c0048): «Whereas, indeed, the cure of spiritual, as of bodily diseases, must be as various as are the causes of them. The first thing, therefore, is to find out the cause; and this will naturally point out the cure.» Reason: Wesley's starting counsel for recovery: identify the cause of the darkness, which points to the cure.
10. #46 The Wilderness State (wesley-046-c0049): «And how can you expect they should return, till you put away the accursed thing?» Reason: Direct counsel: if sin drove away joy and peace, forsake it and the Lord will return and pardon.
11. #46 The Wilderness State (wesley-046-c0057): «It is vain to hope for a recovery of his light, till you pluck out the right eye, and cast it from you. O let there be no longer delay! Cry to Him, that he may enable you so to do!» Reason: How to get the light back when an idol is the cause: cry to God, cast out every idol.
12. #46 The Wilderness State (wesley-046-c0059): «Arise, and shake yourself from the dust; wrestle with God for the mighty blessing; pour out your soul unto God in prayer, and continue therein with all perseverance!» Reason: Cure for a soul gone dead through spiritual sloth: stir up, pray earnestly and persevere.
13. #46 The Wilderness State (wesley-046-c0060): «"Commune with him in your chamber, and be still;" and desire of him to try the ground of your heart, and bring to your remembrance whatever has at any time offended the eyes of his glory.» Reason: Counsel when no present cause is found: ask God to search past sins and renew by repentance and faith.
14. #46 The Wilderness State (wesley-046-c0073): «Joy in the Holy Ghost will far more effectually purify the soul than the want of that joy; and the peace of God is the best means of refining the soul from the dross of earthly affections.» Reason: Rejects the idea that dryness is better for the soul; God's presence and joy, not absence, perfect us.
15. #46 The Wilderness State (wesley-046-c0075): «When either ignorance or sin has caused darkness, one or the other may be removed, and yet the light which was obstructed thereby may not immediately return. As it is the free gift of God, he may restore it, sooner or later, as it pleases him.» Reason: Answers 'can I get it back': God restores the light, though not always immediately after the cause is removed.
16. #46 The Wilderness State (wesley-046-c0078): «And God will then bear witness to his word, and bring their souls out of trouble.» Reason: Promise of restoration: God brings tempted believers out of darkness and their light shines more and more.
17. #21 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 1 (wesley-021-c0071): «This whole process, both of mourning for an absent God, and recovering the joy of his countenance, seems to be shadowed out in what our Lord spoke to his Apostles» Reason: Speaks to mourning a God who seems absent and promises the sorrow will be turned into joy.
18. #28 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 8 (wesley-028-c0009): «Even after God hath opened the eyes of our understanding, if we seek or desire anything else than God, how soon is our foolish heart darkened! Then clouds again rest upon our souls.» Reason: Explains how a once-enlightened heart darkens by seeking other things, and that clouds vanish when we seek God alone.
19. #138 On Grieving the Holy Spirit (wesley-138-c0019): «At those seasons, the blessed Spirit retired and concealed his presence from us, we were justly left to a sense of our own wretchedness and misery, till we humbled ourselves before the Lord» Reason: Grieving the Spirit brings darkness; humbling ourselves with repentance and faith brings back his peace.

column5: Is it gossip if what I say about someone is true? What did Wesley teach about evil-speaking?
column8: #49 The Cure of Evil-speaking, wesley-049-c0001: Matt. 18:15-17 1. "Speak evil of no man," says the great Apostle: -- As plain a command as, "Thou shalt do no murder." But who, even among Christians, regards this command? Yea, how few are there that so much as understand it? What is evil-speaking? It is not, as some suppose, the same with lying or slandering. All a man says may be as true as the Bible; and yet the saying of it is evil-speaking. For «evil-speaking is neither more nor less than speaking evil of an absent person; relating something evil, which was really done or said by one that is not present when it is related.»
column9:
1. #49 The Cure of Evil-speaking (wesley-049-c0007): «Evil-speaking is the more difficult to be avoided, because it frequently attacks us in disguise. We speak thus out of a noble, generous (it is well if we do not say,) holy indignation, against these vile creatures!» Reason: Warns that we excuse talking about others' faults as righteous indignation; it is still sin in disguise.
2. #49 The Cure of Evil-speaking (wesley-049-c0013): «if thou seest with thine own eyes a brother, a fellow Christian, commit undeniable sin, or hearest it with thine own ears, so that it is impossible for thee to doubt the fact, then thy part is plain: Take the very first opportunity of going to him» Reason: Even when the fault is certainly true, Wesley says go to the person privately rather than talk about it.
3. #49 The Cure of Evil-speaking (wesley-049-c0024): «God reproves you for a sin of omission, for not telling your brother of his fault; and you comfort yourself under His reproof by a sin of commission, by telling your brother's fault to another person!» Reason: Answers the 'I just had to tell someone' excuse: telling others instead of the person is itself sin.
4. #49 The Cure of Evil-speaking (wesley-049-c0026): «it is lawful, yea, it is our bounden duty, to speak evil of an absent person, in order to prevent his doing evil to others and himself at the same time. But remember, meanwhile that all evil-speaking is, in its own nature, deadly poison.» Reason: Gives the one exception (to protect others from harm) and insists that otherwise it is deadly poison.
5. #49 The Cure of Evil-speaking (wesley-049-c0050): «But, at the peril of thy soul, tell it to no one else, either before or after, unless in that one exempt case, when it is absolutely needful to preserve the innocent!» Reason: Sums up the rule: tell the person, then witnesses, then the church, and no one else.
6. #49 The Cure of Evil-speaking (wesley-049-c0052): «See that you "speak evil of no man;" of the absent, nothing but good.» Reason: Direct exhortation: put away backbiting and talebearing; say nothing but good of the absent.
7. #14 The Repentance of Believers (wesley-014-c0027): «Of this kind is all backbiting, all tale-bearing, all whispering, all evil-speaking, that is, repeating the faults of absent persons; for none would have others repeat his faults when he is absent.» Reason: Explains why repeating even real faults of absent people is sin: it breaks the golden rule.
8. #22 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 2 (wesley-022-c0070): «So far is he from making the faults or failures of others the matter of his conversation, that of the absent he never does speak at all, unless he can speak well.» Reason: Describes how a loving Christian treats others' known faults: conceals them, speaks of the absent only well.
9. #30 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 10 (wesley-030-c0062): «you will never mention even the real fault of an absent person, unless so far as you are convinced it is absolutely needful for the good of other souls.» Reason: Applies the golden rule: we don't want our real faults published, so don't mention others' real faults.
10. #80 On Friendship with the World (wesley-080-c0018): «We ought to speak no evil of them when they are absent, unless it be absolutely necessary; unless it be the only means we know of preventing their doing hurt» Reason: Counsel on speaking of people behind their backs: no evil unless needed to prevent harm, otherwise speak respectfully.

column5: Romans 8:16
column7: #10 THE WITNESS OF THE SPIRIT, Discourse I
column8: #10 THE WITNESS OF THE SPIRIT, Discourse I, wesley-010-c0000: "«The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God.»" Rom. 8:16 1. How many vain men, not understanding what they spake, neither whereof they affirmed, have wrested this Scripture to the great loss if not the destruction of their souls! How many have mistaken the voice of their own imagination for this witness of the Spirit of God, and thence idly presumed they were the children of God while they were doing the works of the devil! These are truly and properly enthusiasts; and, indeed, in the worst sense of the word. But with what difficulty are they convinced thereof, especially if they have drank deep into that spirit of error!
column9:
1. #10 THE WITNESS OF THE SPIRIT, Discourse I (wesley-010-c0007): «which may be translated, The same Spirit beareth witness to our spirit that we are the children of God (the preposition syn only denoting that he witnesses this at the same time that he enables us to cry Abba, Father.)» Reason: Expounds the Greek of Romans 8:16 and what 'beareth witness with our spirit' means.
2. #10 THE WITNESS OF THE SPIRIT, Discourse I (wesley-010-c0021): «The testimony of the Spirit is an inward impression on the soul, whereby the Spirit of God directly witnesses to my spirit, that I am a child of God» Reason: Wesley's definition of the witness Romans 8:16 describes.
3. #10 THE WITNESS OF THE SPIRIT, Discourse I (wesley-010-c0024): «And we cannot know his pardoning love to us, till his Spirit witnesses it to our spirit. Since, therefore, this testimony of his Spirit must precede the love of God and all holiness» Reason: Explains the order in Romans 8:16: God's Spirit witnesses first, before our own spirit's testimony.
4. #10 THE WITNESS OF THE SPIRIT, Discourse I (wesley-010-c0028): «Should it still be inquired, "How does the Spirit of God bear witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God,' so as to exclude all doubt, and evince the reality of our sonship?"» Reason: Takes up the verse's question of how the Spirit bears witness so as to remove doubt.
5. #10 THE WITNESS OF THE SPIRIT, Discourse I (wesley-010-c0032): «the Spirit of God does give a believer such a testimony of his adoption that while it is present to the soul, he can no more doubt the reality of his sonship, than he can doubt of the shining of the sun» Reason: States the fact Romans 8:16 teaches: the Spirit's testimony makes a believer sure of adoption.
6. #10 THE WITNESS OF THE SPIRIT, Discourse I (wesley-010-c0065): «so surely the witness thou hast in thyself is not of Satan, but of God. 14. Well then mayst thou say, "Thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift!"» Reason: Applies Romans 8:16 to the believer: the witness tested by holiness is from God; give thanks.
7. #11 The Witness of the Spirit, Discourse II (wesley-011-c0046): «To secure us from all delusion, God gives us two witnesses that we are his children. And this they testify conjointly.» Reason: Expounds the two witnesses of Romans 8:16, God's Spirit and ours, jointly guarding against delusion.
8. #18 The Marks of the New Birth (wesley-018-c0024): «This hope implies, First, the testimony of our own spirit or conscience, that we walk "in simplicity and godly sincerity;" Secondly, the testimony of the Spirit of God, "bearing witness with," or to, "our spirit, that we are the children of God,"» Reason: Expounds Romans 8:16 as the two testimonies implied in a Christian's living hope.
9. #18 The Marks of the New Birth (wesley-018-c0028): «though sorrow may precede this witness of God's Spirit with our spirit; (indeed must, in some degree, while we groan under fear, and a sense of the wrath of God abiding on us;) yet, as soon as any man feeleth it in himself, his "sorrow is turned into joy."» Reason: Applies the witness of Romans 8:16 to experience: sorrow before it turns to joy when it is felt.
10. #43 The Scripture Way of Salvation (wesley-043-c0021): «For "he that believeth" with the true living faith "hath the witness in himself": "the Spirit witnesseth with his spirit that he is a child of God."» Reason: Cites Romans 8:16 to show that saving faith carries the Spirit's witness and assurance.
11. #55 On the Trinity (wesley-055-c0037): «till "the Spirit of God witnesses with his spirit, that he is a child of God;" that is, in effect, till God the holy Ghost witnesses that God the Father has accepted him through the merits of God the Son» Reason: Expounds the content of the Romans 8:16 witness in Trinitarian terms.
12. #128 Free Grace (wesley-128-c0026): «the witness of God's Spirit with your spirit that you are a child of God. This, otherwise termed "the full assurance of faith,: is the true ground of a Christian's happiness.» Reason: Explains what the witness of Romans 8:16 implies: present forgiveness and sonship, not necessarily perseverance.
13. #138 On Grieving the Holy Spirit (wesley-138-c0038): «And in order that this inward testimony may be lively and permanent, it is absolutely necessary to attend carefully to the secret operation of the Holy Spirit within us» Reason: Quotes Romans 8:16 and counsels how to keep the Spirit's inward testimony lively.

column5: Christian perfection
column8: #40 Christian Perfection, wesley-040-c0023: 9. «Christian perfection, therefore, does not imply (as some men seem to have imagined) an exemption either from ignorance or mistake, or infirmities or temptations. Indeed, it is only another term for holiness.» They are two names for the same thing. Thus every one that is perfect is holy, and every one that is holy is, in the Scripture sense, perfect. Yet we may, lastly, observe, that neither in this respect is there any absolute perfection on earth. There is no perfection of degrees, as it is termed; none which does not admit of a continual increase. So that how much soever any man hath attained, or in how high a degree soever he is perfect, he hath still need to "grow in grace," [2 Pet. 3:18] and daily to advance in the knowledge and love of God his Saviour. [see Phil. 1:9]
column9:
1. #43 The Scripture Way of Salvation (wesley-043-c0015): «But what is perfection? The word has various senses: here it means perfect love. It is love excluding sin; love filling the heart, taking up the whole capacity of the soul.» Reason: Concise definition of Christian perfection as perfect love excluding sin.
2. #76 On Perfection (wesley-076-c0012): «What is then the perfection of which man is capable while he dwells in a corruptible body? It is the complying with that kind command, "My son, give me thy heart."» Reason: Explains the perfection possible in this life: loving God with all the heart; 'all comprised in that one word, Love.'
3. #76 On Perfection (wesley-076-c0016): «Now, suppose all these to be knit together in one, to be united together in the soul of a believer, this is Christian perfection.» Reason: Describes Christian perfection as the whole fruit of the Spirit united in the believer.
4. #76 On Perfection (wesley-076-c0019): «According to this Apostle, then, perfection is another name for universal holiness: Inward and outward righteousness: Holiness of life, arising from holiness of heart.» Reason: Defines perfection as universal holiness of heart and life.
5. #76 On Perfection (wesley-076-c0023): «And this salvation from sin, from all sin, is another description of perfection; though indeed it expresses only the least, the lowest branch of it, only the negative part of the great salvation.» Reason: Explains perfection as salvation from all sin, and that this is only its negative side.
6. #40 Christian Perfection (wesley-040-c0084): «In conformity, therefore, both to the doctrine of St. John, and to the whole tenor of the New Testament, we fix this conclusion -- A Christian is so far perfect, as not to commit sin.» Reason: States the positive sense in which Christians are perfect: not committing sin, and for mature believers no evil thoughts or tempers.
7. #40 Christian Perfection (wesley-040-c0098): «"True," say some, "we shall thus be saved from our sins; but not till death; not in this world." But how are we to reconcile this with the express words of St. John?» Reason: Defends perfection as attainable in this world, not only at death.
8. #40 Christian Perfection (wesley-040-c0105): «It remains, then, that Christians are saved in this world from all sin, from all unrighteousness; that they are now in such a sense perfect, as not to commit sin, and to be freed from evil thoughts and evil tempers.» Reason: Wesley's summary of the doctrine of Christian perfection in this sermon.
9. #42 Satan's Devices (wesley-042-c0003): «We expect to be "made perfect in love;" in that love which casts out all painful fear, and all desire but that of glorifying him we love, and of loving and serving him more and more.» Reason: Describes what believers expect in Christian perfection: perfect love freeing from fear, anger and pride.
10. #110 On the Discoveries of Faith (wesley-110-c0034): «But what is the "perfection" here spoken of? It is not only a deliverance from doubts and fears, but from sin; from all inward as well as outward sin» Reason: Direct definition of perfection as deliverance from all inward and outward sin.
11. #83 On Patience (wesley-083-c0043): «Ye shall then be perfect. The Apostle seems to mean by this expression, teleioi, ye shall be wholly delivered from every evil work; from every evil word; from every sinful thought; yea, from every evil desire, passion, temper» Reason: Expounds what being perfect means: deliverance from all inbred sin and renewal in God's image.

column5: means of grace
column8: #16 The Means of Grace, wesley-016-c0012: They have probably tried most outward means, and found no ease in them; it may be, more and more of remorse, and fear, and sorrow, and condemnation. It is easy, therefore, to persuade these, that it is better for them to abstain from all those means. They are already weary of striving (as it seems) in vain, of labouring in the fire; and are therefore glad of any pretence to cast aside that wherein their soul has no pleasure, to give over the painful strife, and sink down into an indolent inactivity. II. 1. In the following discourse, I propose to examine at large, whether there are any means of grace. «By "means of grace" I understand outward signs, words, or actions, ordained of God, and appointed for this end, to be the ordinary channels whereby he might convey to men, preventing, justifying, or sanctifying grace.»
column9:
1. #16 The Means of Grace (wesley-016-c0014): «The chief of these means are prayer, whether in secret or with the great congregation; searching the Scriptures; (which implies reading, hearing, and meditating thereon;) and receiving the Lord's Supper» Reason: Names the chief means of grace and says their value lies in leading to the knowledge and love of God.
2. #16 The Means of Grace (wesley-016-c0018): «Whosoever, therefore, imagines there is any intrinsic power in any means whatsoever, does greatly err, not knowing the Scriptures, neither the power of God.» Reason: Key teaching on the means of grace: no power in the means themselves; God alone gives grace through them.
3. #16 The Means of Grace (wesley-016-c0027): «all who desire the grace of God are to wait for it in the means which he hath ordained; in using, not in laying them aside.» Reason: Wesley's thesis on the means of grace: wait for God's grace by using the ordained means.
4. #16 The Means of Grace (wesley-016-c0053): «Is not the eating of that bread, and the drinking of that cup, the outward, visible means, whereby God conveys into our souls all that spiritual grace» Reason: Expounds the Lord's Supper as an ordinary, stated means of grace.
5. #16 The Means of Grace (wesley-016-c0062): «When we say, "Prayer is a means of grace," we understand a channel through which the grace of God is conveyed.» Reason: Defines what calling prayer a means of grace means, answering the objection that Christ is the only means.
6. #16 The Means of Grace (wesley-016-c0083): «whenever opportunity serves, use all the means which God has ordained; for who knows in which God will meet thee with the grace that bringeth salvation?» Reason: Wesley's general rule for the means of grace, and the start of how to use them rightly.
7. #16 The Means of Grace (wesley-016-c0086): «Before you use any means, let it be deeply impressed on your soul; -- there is no power in this. It is, in itself, a poor, dead, empty thing: Separate from God, it is a dry leaf, a shadow.» Reason: Practical rule for using the means of grace: no merit or power in them; use them because God bids.
8. #16 The Means of Grace (wesley-016-c0088): «Remember also, to use all means, as means; as ordained, not for their own sake, but in order to the renewal of your soul in righteousness and true holiness.» Reason: Rule for using the means of grace: seek God alone in them and use them as means, not ends.
9. #4 Scriptural Christianity (wesley-004-c0022): «so he continued daily in all the ordinances of God, the stated channels of his grace to man» Reason: Describes the means of grace as stated channels of grace and shows a believer growing through them.
10. #27 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 7 (wesley-027-c0004): «Some well-meaning men have seemed to place all religion in attending the Prayers of the Church, in receiving the Lord's supper, in hearing sermons, and reading books of piety; neglecting, mean time, the end of all these» Reason: Discusses misuse of the means of grace: mistaking them for the end, which drives others to despise them.
11. #37 The Nature of Enthusiasm (wesley-037-c0065): «Therefore constantly and carefully use all those means which He has appointed to be the ordinary channels of His grace.» Reason: Exhortation to use the appointed means of grace; God could work without them but ordinarily does not.
12. #92 On Zeal (wesley-092-c0017): «By these we exercise all holy tempers- by these we continually improve them, so that all these are real means of grace, although this is not commonly adverted to.» Reason: Extends the means of grace to works of mercy alongside works of piety, and explains how they work.
13. #98 On Visiting the Sick (wesley-098-c0001): «Surely there are works of mercy, as well as works of piety, which are real means of grace.» Reason: Defines the usual means of grace and argues works of mercy are means of grace too; neglect loses grace.

column5: witness of the Spirit
column7: #10 THE WITNESS OF THE SPIRIT, Discourse I
column8: #10 THE WITNESS OF THE SPIRIT, Discourse I, wesley-010-c0021: 7. But what is that testimony of God's Spirit, which is superadded to, and conjoined with, this? How does he "bear witness with our spirit that we are the children of God?" It is hard to find words in the language of men to explain "the deep things of God." Indeed, there are none that will adequately express what the children of God experience. But perhaps one might say, (desiring any who are taught of God to correct, to soften or strengthen the expression,) «The testimony of the Spirit is an inward impression on the soul, whereby the Spirit of God directly witnesses to my spirit, that I am a child of God; that Jesus Christ hath loved me, and given himself for me; and that all my sins are blotted out, and I, even I, am reconciled to God.»
column9:
1. #11 The Witness of the Spirit, Discourse II (wesley-011-c0004): «The testimony now under consideration is given by the Spirit of God to and with our spirit: he is the Person testifying. What he testifies to us is, that we are the children of God. The immediate result of this testimony is, "the fruit of the Spirit;"» Reason: Defines the witness of the Spirit: who testifies, what, and its fruit.
2. #11 The Witness of the Spirit, Discourse II (wesley-011-c0012): «The word of God says, every one who has the fruit of the Spirit is a child of God; experience, or inward consciousness, tells me, that I have the fruit of the Spirit; and hence I rationally conclude, "Therefore I am a child of God."» Reason: Explains the indirect witness, the testimony of our own spirit, alongside the Spirit's.
3. #11 The Witness of the Spirit, Discourse II (wesley-011-c0014): «But the point in question is, whether there be any direct testimony of the Spirit at all; whether there be any other testimony of the Spirit, than that which arises from a consciousness of the fruit.» Reason: States the central question of the doctrine: is there a direct witness beyond the fruit?
4. #11 The Witness of the Spirit, Discourse II (wesley-011-c0023): «The Spirit itself bore witness to my spirit that I was a child of God, gave me an evidence hereof, and I immediately cried, "Abba, Father!" And this I did, (and so did you,) before I reflected on, or was conscious of, any fruit of the Spirit.» Reason: Wesley's own experience confirming the direct witness of the Spirit before any fruit.
5. #11 The Witness of the Spirit, Discourse II (wesley-011-c0036): «And this we do contend for; we contend that the direct witness may shine clear, even while the indirect one is under a cloud.» Reason: Explains how the direct witness relates to the fruit: it may shine when the fruit is clouded.
6. #11 The Witness of the Spirit, Discourse II (wesley-011-c0046): «To secure us from all delusion, God gives us two witnesses that we are his children. And this they testify conjointly.» Reason: Answers the delusion objection: the Spirit's and our spirit's witness together are trustworthy.
7. #11 The Witness of the Spirit, Discourse II (wesley-011-c0050): «The testimony of the Spirit is an inward impression on the souls of believers, whereby the Spirit of God directly testifies to their spirit, that they are children of God.» Reason: Wesley's summary definition of the witness of the Spirit.
8. #11 The Witness of the Spirit, Discourse II (wesley-011-c0055): «The First, let none ever presume to rest in any supposed testimony of the Spirit which is separate from the fruit of it.» Reason: First practical inference: never trust a supposed witness of the Spirit that lacks its fruit.
9. #11 The Witness of the Spirit, Discourse II (wesley-011-c0058): «The Second inference, is, let none rest in any supposed fruit of the Spirit without the witness.» Reason: Second practical inference: do not rest in good fruits without the Spirit's witness of acceptance.
10. #10 THE WITNESS OF THE SPIRIT, Discourse I (wesley-010-c0024): «And we cannot know his pardoning love to us, till his Spirit witnesses it to our spirit. Since, therefore, this testimony of his Spirit must precede the love of God and all holiness» Reason: Explains why the Spirit's witness comes before love and holiness.
11. #10 THE WITNESS OF THE SPIRIT, Discourse I (wesley-010-c0030): «But I thus love, delight, and rejoice in God; Therefore, I am a child of God: -- Then a Christian can in no wise doubt of his being a child of God.» Reason: Explains the witness of our own spirit that joins with the Spirit's witness.
12. #10 THE WITNESS OF THE SPIRIT, Discourse I (wesley-010-c0032): «the Spirit of God does give a believer such a testimony of his adoption that while it is present to the soul, he can no more doubt the reality of his sonship, than he can doubt of the shining of the sun» Reason: Affirms the fact of the Spirit's witness and its certainty, though its manner is beyond explanation.
13. #10 THE WITNESS OF THE SPIRIT, Discourse I (wesley-010-c0036): «I answer, the Holy Scriptures abound with marks, whereby the one may be distinguished from the other.» Reason: Begins Wesley's account of how the true witness is distinguished from presumption.
14. #10 THE WITNESS OF THE SPIRIT, Discourse I (wesley-010-c0061): «By the fruits which he hath wrought in your spirit, you shall know the testimony of the Spirit of God. Hereby you shall know, that you are in no delusion, that you have not deceived your own soul.» Reason: Gives the test of a genuine witness of the Spirit: the fruits it produces.
15. #18 The Marks of the New Birth (wesley-018-c0024): «Who is it that is here said to bear witness? Not our spirit only, but another; even the Spirit of God: He it is who "beareth witness with our spirit." What is it he beareth witness of?» Reason: Expounds the witness of the Spirit: who bears it, what it testifies, and to whom.
16. #55 On the Trinity (wesley-055-c0037): «till "the Spirit of God witnesses with his spirit, that he is a child of God;" that is, in effect, till God the holy Ghost witnesses that God the Father has accepted him through the merits of God the Son» Reason: Says no one is a Christian believer without the Spirit's witness, and explains its content.
17. #138 On Grieving the Holy Spirit (wesley-138-c0038): «And in order that this inward testimony may be lively and permanent, it is absolutely necessary to attend carefully to the secret operation of the Holy Spirit within us» Reason: Counsel on keeping the witness of the Spirit lively by attending to the Spirit within.

column5: Gain all you can
column8: #50 The Use of Money, wesley-050-c0011: It is therefore of the highest concern that all who fear God know how to employ this valuable talent; that they be instructed how it may answer these glorious ends, and in the highest degree. And, perhaps, all the instructions which are necessary for this may be reduced to three plain rules, by the exact observance whereof we may approve ourselves faithful stewards of "the mammon of unrighteousness." I. 1. The first of these is «(he that heareth, let him understand!) "Gain all you can." Here we may speak like the children of the world: We meet them on their own ground.» And it is our bounden duty to do this: We ought to gain all we can gain, without buying gold too dear, without paying more for it than it is worth.
column9:
1. #50 The Use of Money (wesley-050-c0016): «We are, Secondly, to gain all we can without hurting our mind any more than our body. For neither may we hurt this. We must preserve, at all events, the spirit of an healthful mind. Therefore we may not engage or continue in any sinful trade» Reason: Expounds the rule's second limit: gain all you can without harming your mind or entering a sinful trade.
2. #50 The Use of Money (wesley-050-c0020): «We are. Thirdly, to gain all we can without hurting our neighbour. But this we may not, cannot do, if we love our neighbour as ourselves. We cannot, if we love everyone as ourselves, hurt anyone in his substance.» Reason: Expounds the rule's third limit: gain all you can without hurting your neighbour.
3. #50 The Use of Money (wesley-050-c0032): «it is the bounden duty of all who are engaged in worldly business to observe that first and great rule of Christian wisdom with respect to money, "Gain all you can." Gain all you can by honest industry. Use all possible diligence in your calling. Lose no time.» Reason: States the rule positively: gain all you can by honest industry and diligence in your calling.
4. #50 The Use of Money (wesley-050-c0034): «Gain all you can, by common sense, by using in your business all the understanding which God has given you. It is amazing to observe, how few do this; how men run on in the same dull track with their forefathers.» Reason: Expounds the rule further: gain all you can by using your God-given understanding and improving your work.
5. #50 The Use of Money (wesley-050-c0048): «But let not any man imagine that he has done anything, barely by going thus far, by "gaining and saving all he can," if he were to stop here. All this is nothing, if a man go not forward, if he does not point all this at a farther end.» Reason: Key qualification of 'gain all you can': it is worthless unless directed to giving.
6. #50 The Use of Money (wesley-050-c0061): «Gain all you can, without hurting either yourself or your neighbour, in soul or body, by applying hereto with unintermitted diligence, and with all the understanding which God has given you» Reason: Wesley's summary of the rule with its limits, joined to saving and giving.
7. #68 The Wisdom of God's Counsels (wesley-068-c0041): «They gain all they can, honestly and conscientiously. They save all they can, by cutting off all needless expense; by adding frugality to diligence. And so far all is right. This is the duty of every one that fears God. But they do not give all they can» Reason: Restates the rule as a duty while warning that gaining without giving makes people earthly-minded.
8. #87 The Danger of Riches (wesley-087-c0044): «And is it possible to do this without both desiring and endeavouring to be rich? nay, suppose our endeavours are successful, without actually laying up treasures upon earth?" I answer, It is possible. You may gain all you can without hurting either your soul or body» Reason: Wesley answers whether 'gain all you can' means seeking riches: no, if one never lays up treasure.
9. #116 Causes of the Inefficacy of Christianity (wesley-116-c0022): «Of the three rules which are laid down on this head, in the sermon on "The Mammon of Unrighteousness," you may find many that observe the First rule, namely, "Gain all you can."» Reason: Wesley reflects on how his rule 'Gain all you can' was kept while the rule to give was neglected.
10. #116 Causes of the Inefficacy of Christianity (wesley-116-c0046): «Do you gain all you can, and save all you can? Then you must, in the nature of things, grow rich. Then if you have any desire to escape the damnation of hell, give all you can» Reason: Applies the rule: gaining and saving make one rich, so giving all one can must follow.
11. #126 On the Danger of Increasing Riches (wesley-126-c0038): «After you have gained (with the cautions above given) all you can, and saved all you can, wanting for nothing; spend not one pound, one shilling, or one penny, to gratify either the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, or the pride of life» Reason: Restates gain all you can with its cautions and the giving that must follow it.

column5: Philippians 3:12
column8: #40 Christian Perfection, wesley-040-c0000: "«Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect.»" Phil. 3:12. 1. There is scarce any expression in Holy Writ which has given more offence than this. The word perfect is what many cannot bear. The very sound of it is an abomination to them. And whosoever preaches perfection (as the phrase is,) that is, asserts that it is attainable in this life, runs great hazard of being accounted by them worse than a heathen man or a publican. 2. And hence some have advised, wholly to lay aside the use of those expressions, "because they have given so great offence." But are they not found in the oracles of God?
column9:
1. #40 Christian Perfection (wesley-040-c0003): «the Apostle speaks of himself as not perfect: "Not," saith he, "as though I were already perfect." And yet immediately after, in the fifteenth verse, he speaks of himself, yea and many others, as perfect.» Reason: Expounds Phil 3:12 directly: Paul calls himself not perfect yet perfect in v.15; Wesley sets out to resolve this.
2. #40 Christian Perfection (wesley-040-c0023): «Christian perfection, therefore, does not imply (as some men seem to have imagined) an exemption either from ignorance or mistake, or infirmities or temptations.» Reason: Wesley's resolution of the verse: the sense in which Christians are 'not already perfect' (no absolute perfection; still need to grow).
3. #42 Satan's Devices (wesley-042-c0061): «Rejoice in having a fresh proof of the faithfulness of God in fulfilling all his promises; and stir yourself up the more, to "apprehend that for which you also are apprehended of Christ Jesus!"» Reason: Quotes Phil 3:12's 'apprehend that for which' and applies it: press on toward perfect love yourself.

column5: 1 Corinthians 10:13
column8: #82 On Temptation, wesley-082-c0000: "«There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: And God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.»" 1 Cor. 10:13. 1. In the foregoing part of the chapter, the Apostle has been reciting, on the one hand, the unparalleled mercies of God to the Israelites; and, on the other, the unparalleled ingratitude of that disobedient and gainsaying people. [1 Cor. 10:1-10] And all these things, as the Apostle observes, "were written for our ensample;" [1 Cor. 10:11] that we might take warning from them, so as to avoid their grievous sins, and escape their terrible punishment.
column9:
1. #82 On Temptation (wesley-082-c0009): «lest the fearful of heart should be utterly cast down, supposing it impossible for them to stand; the Apostle subjoins to that serious exhortation, these comfortable words: There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man» Reason: Quotes the verse in full and explains its purpose: comfort for the fearful after the warning of verse 12.
2. #82 On Temptation (wesley-082-c0012): «"Such as is suited to the nature and circumstances of man; such as every man may reasonably expect, if he considers the nature of his body and his soul, and his situation in the present world."» Reason: Expounds 'common to man' (anthropinos): temptation suited to human nature, so we should not be surprised by it.
3. #82 On Temptation (wesley-082-c0028): «what a comfort it is to know, with the utmost certainty, that "God is faithful, who will not suffer us to be tempted above what we are able." He knoweth what our ability is, and cannot be mistaken.» Reason: Expounds 'God is faithful... not above that ye are able': God knows our strength and proportions temptation to it.
4. #82 On Temptation (wesley-082-c0033): «He sees exactly how much we can endure with our present degree of strength. And if this is not sufficient, he can increase it to whatever degree it pleases him.» Reason: Expounds the verse's promise: God watches our strength and gives more as needed, so we are never tempted beyond it.
5. #82 On Temptation (wesley-082-c0035): «It literally means a way out. And this God will either find our make; which He that hath all wisdom, as well as all power in heaven and earth, can never be at a loss how to do.» Reason: Explains the Greek 'ekbasin' (way to escape) and the two ways God makes it: out of or within the temptation.
6. #82 On Temptation (wesley-082-c0044): «Thus is God able to deliver out of temptation, by taking away the very ground of it. And he is equally able to deliver in the temptation; which, perhaps, is the greatest deliverance of all.» Reason: Expounds the 'way to escape' as deliverance either out of or within the temptation.
7. #82 On Temptation (wesley-082-c0052): «lest he say in his hear, "Surely no one's case is like mine; no one was ever tried like me." Yea, ten thousand. "There was no temptation taken you," but such as is "common to man;"» Reason: Applies 'common to man': do not murmur that your trial is unique; it is the common lot of humanity.
8. #82 On Temptation (wesley-082-c0054): «Not so; unless something is too hard for God. He will not suffer you to be "tempted above that ye are able." He proportions the burden to your strength. If you want more strength, "ask, and it shall be given you."» Reason: Applies the verse against despair: God proportions the burden to your strength; ask for more.
9. #82 On Temptation (wesley-082-c0055): «Let us then receive every trial with calm resignation, and with humble confidence that He who hath all power, all wisdom, all mercy, and all faithfulness, will first support us in every temptation, and then deliver us out of all» Reason: Closing application of the verse: trust God's faithfulness to support in and deliver from every temptation.
10. #29 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 9 (wesley-029-c0075): «But when the temptation comes, the grace will come. In greater trials you will have greater strength.» Reason: Applies the verse in another sermon: grace comes with the temptation, and God makes a way to escape.
11. #40 Christian Perfection (wesley-040-c0061): «With the temptation which fell on them, there was a way to escape; as there is to every soul of man in every temptation. So that whosoever is tempted to any sin, need not yield» Reason: Cites 1 Cor 10:13 to argue that no one tempted need yield to sin, since a way to escape always exists.

column5: Matthew 6:34
column7: #29 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 9
column8: #29 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 9, wesley-029-c0003: But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you. "«Take therefore no thought for the morrow: For the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.»'" Matt. 6:24-34. 1. It is recorded of the nations whom the King of Assyria, after he had carried Israel away into captivity, placed in the cities of Samaria, that "they feared the Lord, and served their own gods." "These nations," saith the inspired writer, "feared the Lord;" performed an outward service to him (a plain proof that they had a fear of God, though not according to knowledge;) "and served their graven images, both their children, and their children's children: As did their fathers, so do they unto this day. (2 Kings 17:33.)
column9:
1. #29 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 9 (wesley-029-c0041): «He forbids only that care which poisons the blessings of to-day, by fear of what may be to-morrow; which cannot enjoy the present plenty, through apprehensions of future want.» Reason: Expounds what 'take no thought' forbids: anxious care that poisons today with fear of tomorrow.
2. #29 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 9 (wesley-029-c0061): «"Therefore take no thought for the morrow." Not only, take ye no thought how to lay up treasures on earth, how to increase in worldly substance» Reason: Quotes Matthew 6:34 and begins Wesley's exposition of its meaning: no uneasy thought even for needful things.
3. #29 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 9 (wesley-029-c0064): «Above all, do not make the care of future things a pretence for neglecting present duty. This is the most fatal way of "taking thought for the morrow."» Reason: Expounds the verse: the worst way of taking thought for the morrow is neglecting present duty.
4. #29 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 9 (wesley-029-c0068): «There is another way of "taking thought for the morrow," which is equally forbidden in these words. It is possible to take thought in a wrong manner, even with regard to spiritual things» Reason: Expounds the verse as also forbidding spiritual putting-off: neglecting what God requires now.
5. #29 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 9 (wesley-029-c0074): «And take no thought for the temptations of to-morrow. This also is a dangerous snare. Think not, "When such a temptation comes, what shall I do? how shall I stand?» Reason: Applies the verse to fear of future temptations, which Wesley calls a snare.
6. #29 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 9 (wesley-029-c0076): «"Let the morrow," therefore, "take thought for the things of itself;" that is, when the morrow comes, then think of it. Live thou to-day.» Reason: Direct exposition of the verse's middle clause: think of tomorrow when it comes; live today.
7. #29 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 9 (wesley-029-c0080): «"Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof." Evil it is, speaking after the manner of men; whether it be reproach or want, pain or sickness; but in the language of God, all is blessing» Reason: Expounds the verse's last clause: each day's evil is apportioned by God and is blessing.
8. #26 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 6 (wesley-026-c0064): «"This day:" -- For we are to take no thought for the morrow. For this very end has our wise Creator divided life into these little portions of time» Reason: Applies 'take no thought for the morrow' to the Lord's Prayer: each day is a fresh gift to devote to God.

column5: 2 Corinthians 2:11
column8: #42 Satan's Devices, wesley-042-c0000: "«We are not ignorant of his devices.»" 2 Cor. 2:11. 1. The devices whereby the subtle god of this world labours to destroy the children of God -- or at least to torment whom he cannot destroy, to perplex and hinder them in running the race which is set before them -- are numberless as the stars of heaven or the sand upon the sea-shore. But it is of one of them only that I now propose to speak, (although exerted in various ways,) whereby he endeavours to divide the gospel against itself, and by one part of it to overthrow the other. 2.
column9:
1. #42 Satan's Devices (wesley-042-c0007): «Now this is the grand device of Satan, to destroy the first work of God in the soul, or at least to hinder its increase, by our expectation of that greater work.» Reason: States the device Wesley expounds from 2 Cor 2:11 and his plan to show how to retort it.
2. #42 Satan's Devices (wesley-042-c0012): «If he can prevail thus far, if he can damp our joy, he will soon attack our peace also. He will suggest, "Are you fit to see God?» Reason: Expounds one of Satan's devices from the text: after damping joy, he attacks the believer's peace.
3. #42 Satan's Devices (wesley-042-c0019): «But his master-piece of subtlety is still behind. Not content to strike at your peace and joy, he will carry his attempts farther yet: He will level his assault against your righteousness also.» Reason: Expounds Satan's chief device in this sermon on 2 Cor 2:11: undermining present holiness.
4. #42 Satan's Devices (wesley-042-c0035): «Thus does the subtle adversary of God and man endeavour to make void the counsel of God, by dividing the gospel against itself, and making one part of it overthrow the other» Reason: Wesley's summary of the device he expounds from 2 Cor 2:11: setting the gospel against itself.
5. #42 Satan's Devices (wesley-042-c0044): «You may cast back this dart upon his own head, while through the grace of God, the more you feel of your own vileness, the more you rejoice in confident hope, that all this shall be done away.» Reason: Applies the text: how believers who know Satan's devices can turn his darts back on him.
6. #27 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 7 (wesley-027-c0001): «It has been the endeavour of Satan, from the beginning of the world, to put asunder what God hath joined together; to separate inward from outward religion; to set one of these at variance with the other. And herein he has met with no small success among those who were "ignorant of his devices."» Reason: Quotes 'ignorant of his devices' and expounds a specific device: setting inward against outward religion.
7. #120 On the Wedding Garment (wesley-120-c0021): «It may be of use to enumerate some of them, lest ye should be ignorant of Satan's devices.» Reason: Borderline: cites 2 Cor 2:11 to introduce Satan's counterfeits of holiness, such as idolatry passed off as piety.

column5: Luke 22:19
column7: #101 The Duty of Constant Communion J.W.
column8: #101 The Duty of Constant Communion J.W., wesley-101-c0000: "«Do this in remembrance of me.»" Luke 22:19. It is no wonder that men who have no fear of God should never think of doing this. But it is strange that it should be neglected by any that do fear God, and desire to save their souls; And yet nothing is more common. One reason why many neglect it is, they are so much afraid of "eating and drinking unworthily," that they never think how much greater the danger is when they do not eat or drink it at all. That I may do what I can to bring these well-meaning men to a more just way of thinking, I shall,
column9:
1. #101 The Duty of Constant Communion J.W. (wesley-101-c0002): «"Do this in remembrance of me:" By which, as the Apostles were obliged to bless, break, and give the bread to all that joined with them in holy things; so were all Christians obliged to receive those sign of Christ's body and blood.» Reason: Expounds Luke 22:19 as a standing command binding all Christians to receive the bread and wine to the end of the world.
2. #101 The Duty of Constant Communion J.W. (wesley-101-c0004): «A Second reason why every Christian should do this as often as he can, is, because the benefits of doing it are so great to all that do it in obedience to him» Reason: Continues the exposition of 'Do this': the benefits of obeying it are forgiveness and strengthening of the soul.
3. #101 The Duty of Constant Communion J.W. (wesley-101-c0010): «Hence we learn that the design of this sacrament is, the continual remembrance of the death of Christ, by eating bread and drinking wine, which are the outward signs of the inward grace» Reason: Explains what 'in remembrance of me' means: the Supper's design is continual remembrance of Christ's death.
4. #16 The Means of Grace (wesley-016-c0050): «"This do in remembrance of me." Likewise, "he took the cup, saying, This cup is the new testament," or covenant, "in my blood;" the sacred sign of that covenant» Reason: Quotes the institution words and expounds them: the bread and cup are sacred signs showing forth the Lord's death.
5. #85 On Working out our own Salvation (wesley-085-c0025): «At every opportunity, be a partaker of the Lord's Supper. "Do this in remembrance of him: and he will meet you at his own table.» Reason: Applies the verse directly: receive at every opportunity, with the promise that Christ meets us at his table.

column8: #16 The Means of Grace, wesley-016-c0079 (proposed): To one who begins to feel the weight of his sins, not only hearing the Word of God, but reading it too, and perhaps other serious books, may be a means of deeper conviction. May you not advise him also, to meditate on what he reads, that it may have its full force upon his heart? Yea, and to speak thereof, and not be ashamed, particularly among those who walk in the same path. When trouble and heaviness take hold upon him, should you not then earnestly exhort him to «pour out his soul before God; "always to pray and not to faint;" and when he feels the worthlessness of his own prayers, are you not to work together with God, and remind him of going up into the house of the Lord», and praying with all ! ! that fear him? Reason: Speaks to one who feels his prayers are worthless: keep pouring out your soul, do not faint, and pray alongside other believers.
column9:
1. #16 The Means of Grace (wesley-016-c0076): «to pray to him; although, through fear and shame, he scarce knows what to say. But whether he can speak or no, he cannot but pray, were it only in "groans which cannot be uttered."» Reason: For one who scarcely knows what to say to God: prayer can be wordless groaning, and that still counts.
2. #26 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 6 (wesley-026-c0018): «Prayer is the lifting up of the heart to God: All words of prayer, without this, are mere hypocrisy. Whenever therefore thou attemptest to pray, see that it be thy one design to commune with God, to lift up thy heart to him, to pour out thy soul before him» Reason: Explains what prayer really is (lifting the heart, pouring out the soul), a basic answer to 'I don't know how to pray.'
3. #26 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 6 (wesley-026-c0026): «So that the end of your praying is not to inform God, as though he knew not your wants already; but rather to inform yourselves; to fix the sense of those wants more deeply in your hearts» Reason: Reframes what prayer is for when nothing seems to come back: it shapes the one praying, not informs God.
4. #89 The More Excellent Way (wesley-089-c0023): «In like manner you may suit your devotions to your inward state, the present state of your mind. Is your soul in heaviness, either from a sense of sin, or through manifold temptations? Then let your prayer consist of such confessions, petitions, and supplications, as are agreeable to your distressed situation of mind.» Reason: Practical advice on how to pray when the soul is heavy: fit your prayer to your actual state instead of a stale form.
5. #46 The Wilderness State (wesley-046-c0059): «O stir yourself up before the Lord! Arise, and shake yourself from the dust; wrestle with God for the mighty blessing; pour out your soul unto God in prayer, and continue therein with all perseverance!» Reason: Counsel for a soul that feels dead toward God: keep wrestling in prayer and persevere rather than settle into dryness.
6. #21 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 1 (wesley-021-c0070): «Blessed are they who "follow on to know the Lord," and steadily refuse all other comfort. They shall be comforted by the consolations of his Spirit; by a fresh manifestation of his love» Reason: Promise to those mourning a God who seems hidden: keep seeking him and he will again make his love felt.
7. #141 On the Holy Spirit (wesley-141-c0059): «And the abiding sense of this may possibly become a prayer in the ears of the Most High; -- a prayer not resulting from a set of speculative notions, but from the real, undissembled state of all that is within me» Reason: Says an honest, felt sense of need can itself be a prayer God hears, even without the right words.

column8: #47 Heaviness through Manifold Temptations, wesley-047-c0028 (proposed): Were it not that he is restrained by an unseen hand, would he not soon "curse God and die?" O want of bread! want of bread! Who can tell what this means unless he hath felt it himself? I am astonished it occasions no more than heaviness even in them that believe! 4. Perhaps, next to this, «we may place the death of those who were near and dear unto us; of a tender parent, and one not much declined into the vale of years»; of a beloved child, just rising into life, and clasping about our heart; of a friend that was as our own soul, -- next the grace of God, the last, best gift of Heaven. Reason: Names the death of a parent as one of the deepest causes of heaviness; the passage goes on to say God means us to grieve.
column9:
1. #47 Heaviness through Manifold Temptations (wesley-047-c0014): «Neither does this appear to be a transient sorrow, such as passes away in an hour; but rather, such as, having taken fast hold of the heart, is not presently shaken off, but continues for some time» Reason: Says deep sorrow often lingers for a season even in faithful people; speaks to why the sadness hasn't lifted yet.
2. #135 On Mourning for the Dead (wesley-135-c0005): «Be it my comfort, my constant comfort, when my sorrows bear hard upon me, that I shall shortly, very shortly, go to him!» Reason: Comfort for a mourner when sorrow presses hard: the hope of going to and seeing the loved one again.
3. #135 On Mourning for the Dead (wesley-135-c0016): «"I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep; that ye sorrow not, even as others who have no hope.» Reason: Applies 1 Thessalonians 4 to grief for the dead, calling it the only word that gives lasting comfort to a wounded spirit.
4. #135 On Mourning for the Dead (wesley-135-c0026): «What can give us sufficient ease after that rupture, which has left such an aching void in our breasts? What, indeed, but the reflection already mentioned, which can never be inculcated too often, -- that we are hastening to him ourselves» Reason: Speaks directly to the 'aching void' after losing someone close and names what eases it: we will soon follow them.
5. #135 On Mourning for the Dead (wesley-135-c0029): «If we are, at any time, in danger of being overcome by dwelling too long on the gloomy side of this prospect, to the giving us pain, the making us unfit for the duties and offices of life» Reason: Counsel for grief that disrupts daily duties (like work): turn to the bright side, the coming resurrection.

column5: We are so broke. I feel guilty buying the kids anything that isn't on sale. What are we supposed to do with money when there isn't enough?
column8: #50 The Use of Money, wesley-050-c0053 (proposed): If you desire to be a faithful and a wise steward, out of that portion of your Lord's goods which he has for the present lodged in your hands, but with the right of resuming whenever it pleases him, «First, provide things needful for yourself; food to eat, raiment to put on, whatever nature moderately requires for preserving the body in health and strength. Secondly, provide these for your wife, your children, your servants, or any others who pertain to your household.» If when this is done there be an overplus left, then "do good to them that are of the household of faith." If there be an overplus still, "as you have opportunity, do good unto all men." In so doing, you give all you can; nay, in a sound sense, all you have: For all that is laid out in this manner is really given to God. Reason: Wesley's order for using money: first your own and your children's real needs; spending on them is part of serving God, not a guilty extra.
column9:
1. #50 The Use of Money (wesley-050-c0054): «If, then, a doubt should at any time arise in your mind concerning what you are going to expend, either on yourself or any part of your family, you have an easy way to remove it.» Reason: Speaks to guilt or doubt over a purchase for the family and gives simple steward's questions to settle it.
2. #29 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 9 (wesley-029-c0043): «Take no uneasy thought: This is a plain, sure rule, Uneasy care is unlawful care. With a single eye to God, do all that in you lies to provide things honest in the sight of all men. And then give up all into better hands; leave the whole event to God.» Reason: Counsel for money anxiety: do what you honestly can to provide, then leave the outcome to God instead of fretting.
3. #29 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 9 (wesley-029-c0063): «Why should you perplex yourself without need? God provides for you to-day what is needful to sustain the life which he hath given you. It is enough: Give yourself up into his hands. If you live another day, he will provide for that also.» Reason: Comfort when there isn't enough: God supplies today's needs and will provide again tomorrow.

column7: #70 The Case of Reason Impartially Considered
column8: #70 The Case of Reason Impartially Considered, wesley-070-c0051 (proposed): But, at the same time, acknowledge it is utterly incapable of giving either faith, or hope, or love; and, consequently, of producing either real virtue, or substantial happiness. Expect these from a higher source, even from the Father of the spirits of all flesh. «Seek and receive them, not as your own acquisition, but as the gifts of God. Lift up your hearts to Him who "giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not." He alone can give that faith, which is "the evidence" and conviction "of things not seen."» He alone can "beget you unto a lively hope" of an inheritance eternal in the heavens; and He alone can "shed his love abroad in your heart by the Holy Ghost given unto you." Ask, therefore, and it shall be given you! Reason: For someone who can't make themselves believe: faith is a gift God gives to those who ask, not something you manufacture.
column9:
1. #16 The Means of Grace (wesley-016-c0083): «the sure and general rule for all who groan for the salvation of God is this, -whenever opportunity serves, use all the means which God has ordained; for who knows in which God will meet thee with the grace that bringeth salvation?» Reason: Encourages a struggling seeker to keep attending worship and other means, since God may meet them there.
2. #2 The Almost Christian (wesley-002-c0040): «Awake, then, thou that sleepest, and call upon thy God: call in the day when he may be found. Let him not rest, till he make his "goodness to pass before thee;"» Reason: To one who has the outward form but not living faith: don't settle for going through the motions; keep calling on God.

column7: #8 THE FIRST FRUITS OF THE SPIRIT
column8: #8 THE FIRST FRUITS OF THE SPIRIT, wesley-008-c0041 (proposed): And, first, if there be "no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus," and "walk not after the flesh , but after the Spirit," on account of their past sin; then why art thou fearful, O thou of little faith? «Though thy sins were once more in number than the sand, what is that to thee, now thou art in Christ Jesus? "Who shall lay anything to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifieth: Who is he that condemneth?"» all the sins thou hast committed from thy youth up, until the hour when thou wast "accepted in the Beloved," are driven away as chaff, are gone, are lost, swallowed up, remembered no more. Reason: Speaks to lingering guilt over old sin: in Christ past sins are gone and remembered no more, so stop living under them.
column9:
1. #8 THE FIRST FRUITS OF THE SPIRIT (wesley-008-c0044): «At whatsoever time thou truly believest in the name of the Son of God, all thy sins, antecedent to that hour, vanish away as the morning dew.» Reason: Assures that whenever one truly believes, every earlier sin is cancelled; the person need not keep carrying it.
2. #46 The Wilderness State (wesley-046-c0060): «If the guilt of any unrepented sin remain on our soul, it cannot be but you will remain in darkness, till, having been renewed by repentance, you are again washed by faith in the "fountain opened for sin and uncleanness."» Reason: Explains why an old sin can still leave one feeling unclean, and the cure: repent of it and be washed by faith.
3. #7 The Way to the Kingdom (wesley-007-c0051): «"He pardoneth and absolveth all that truly repent, and unfeignedly believe his holy gospel." As soon as ever God hath spoken to thy heart, "Be of good cheer, thy sins are forgiven thee," his kingdom comes» Reason: Plain promise that God pardons all who repent and believe; the answer to carrying hidden guilt.
4. #5 Justification By Faith (wesley-005-c0023): «"Blessed are they," saith he, "whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered: Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin." To him that is justified or forgiven, God "will not impute sin" to his condemnation.» Reason: Explains that forgiveness means God no longer counts the sin against you; addresses ongoing self-condemnation.
5. #6 The Righteousness of Faith (wesley-006-c0022): «"thou shalt be saved" from condemnation, from the guilt and punishment of thy former sins, and shalt have power to serve God in true holiness all the remaining days of thy life.» Reason: Promises release from the guilt of former sins by faith, plus power to live differently afterward.

column5: I yelled at my kids again tonight and I saw the look on my daughter's face. I don't want to be this angry.
column8: #139 On Love, wesley-139-c0028 (proposed): By happiness I mean, not a slight, trilling pleasure, that perhaps begins and ends in the same hour; but such a state of well-being as contents the soul, and gives it a stead, lasting satisfaction. But that nothing without love can profit us, as to our present happiness, will appear from this single consideration: You cannot want it, in any one single instance, without pain; and the more you depart from it, the pain is the greater. Are you wanting in longsuffering? Then, so far as you fall short of this, you fall short of happiness. «The more the opposite tempers -- anger, fretfulness, revenge -- prevail, the more unhappy you are. You know it; you feel it; nor can the storm be allayed, or peace ever return to your soul, unless meekness, gentleness, patience, or, in one word, love, take possession of it.» Reason: Names the misery that anger brings and the only cure: love, meekness and patience taking hold of the heart.
column9:
1. #22 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 2 (wesley-022-c0006): «They do not desire to extinguish any of the passions which God has for wise ends implanted in their nature; but they have the mastery of all: They hold them all in subjection» Reason: Describes the goal for an angry person: not to feel nothing, but to have meekness 'hold the reins' over anger.
2. #33 UPON OUR LORD'S SERMON ON THE MOUNT, Discourse 13 (wesley-033-c0050): «Hold an even scale as to all your passions, but in particular, as to anger, sorrow, and fear. Calmly acquiesce in whatsoever is the will of God. Learn in every state wherein you are, therewith to be content. Be mild to the good: Be gentle toward all men» Reason: Direct exhortation to govern anger in particular and be gentle with everyone, including at home.
3. #22 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 2 (wesley-022-c0019): «"Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother," (at least do all that in thee lies toward being reconciled,) "and then come and offer thy gift."» Reason: After hurting someone through anger, go and make it right quickly; fits repairing things with a child after yelling.
4. #65 The Duty of Reproving our Neighbour (wesley-065-c0025): «Anger, though it be adorned with the name of zeal, begets anger; not love or holiness. We should therefore avoid, with all possible care, the very appearance of it. Let there be no trace of it, either in the eyes, the gesture, or the tone of voice» Reason: On correcting others: anger breeds anger, not goodness, so correct without a raised voice; fits disciplining children.
5. #9 The Spirit of Bondage and of Adoption. (wesley-009-c0057): «It is by him they are delivered from anger and pride, from all vile and inordinate affections.» Reason: Hope for someone who can't stop being angry: God's Spirit delivers from anger, not just willpower.
6. #43 The Scripture Way of Salvation (wesley-043-c0011): «they feel in themselves sometimes pride or self-will, sometimes anger or unbelief. They find one or more of these frequently stirring in their heart, though not conquering; yea, perhaps, "thrusting sore at them that they may fall"; but the Lord is their help.» Reason: Explains that anger keeps surfacing even in sincere believers, and that God helps them resist it.

column7: #65 The Duty of Reproving our Neighbour
column8: #65 The Duty of Reproving our Neighbour, wesley-065-c0038 (proposed): "Sinners of every other sort," said a venerable old Clergyman, "have I frequently known converted to God. But an habitual drunkard I have never known converted." «But I have known five hundred, perhaps five thousand. Ho! Art thou one who readest these words? Then hear thou the words of the Lord! I have a message from God unto thee, O sinner! Thus saith the Lord, Cast not away thy hope. I have not forgotten thee.» He that tells thee there is no help is a liar from the beginning. Look up! Behold the Lamb of God, who taketh away the sin of the world! This day is salvation come to thy soul: Only see that thou despise not him that speaketh! Reason: Wesley speaks straight to the habitual drinker: he has seen thousands set free, so don't give up hope; God hasn't forgotten you.
column9:
1. #9 The Spirit of Bondage and of Adoption. (wesley-009-c0037): «And the more he frets against it, the more it prevails; he may bite but cannot break his chain. Thus he toils without end, repenting and sinning, and repenting and sinning again» Reason: Explains the cycle of resolving and relapsing into a besetting sin: willpower alone cannot break the chain.
2. #9 The Spirit of Bondage and of Adoption. (wesley-009-c0045): «until the time that God answers the wretched man, crying out, "Who shall deliver me" from this bondage of sin, from this body of death? -- "The grace of God, through Jesus Christ thy Lord."» Reason: Names the way out of the repeat-and-fail cycle: deliverance comes by God's grace in Christ, not by trying harder.
3. #78 Spiritual Idolatry (wesley-078-c0043): «But do not either resolve, or attempt to execute your resolution, trusting in your own strength. If you do, you will be utterly foiled. You are not able to contend with the evil world, much less with your own evil heart» Reason: Speaks to failed public resolutions: resolving in your own strength fails; cry to God for strength instead.

column8: #107 On God's Vineyard, wesley-107-c0060 (proposed): It is well if this bad wisdom was not one cause of your bringing forth wild grapes! 6. «Was not another cause of it your despising that excellent help, union with a Christian society? Have you not read, "How can one be warm alone?" and, "Woe be unto him that is alone when he falleth?"» But you have companions enough. Perhaps more than enough; more than are helpful to your soul. But have you enough that are athirst for God, and that labour to make you so? Have you companions enough that watch over your soul, as they that must give account; and that freely and faithfully warn you, if you take any false step, or are in danger of doing so? Reason: Wesley warns against going it alone and urges union with a Christian society; speaks to having no one close.
column9: 1. #28 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 8 (wesley-028-c0066): «He is a very present help in time of trouble such an help as can never fail. Then shalt thou say, if all thy other friends die, "The Lord liveth, and blessed be my strong helper!"» Reason: When human friends fail or are absent, God is a present help who never fails; direct comfort for someone with no one.

column8: #50 The Use of Money, wesley-050-c0013 (proposed): Therefore, no gain whatsoever should induce us to enter into, or to continue in, any employ, which is of such a kind, or is «attended with so hard or so long labour, as to impair our constitution. Neither should we begin or continue in any business which necessarily deprives us of proper seasons for food and sleep, in such a proportion as our nature requires.» Indeed, there is a great difference here. Some employments are absolutely and totally unhealthy; as those which imply the dealing much with arsenic, or other equally hurtful minerals, or the breathing an air tainted with steams of melting lead, which must at length destroy the firmest constitution. Reason: Wesley says no work is worth wrecking your health or losing food and sleep; overwork is not a duty.
column9:
1. #24 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 4 (wesley-024-c0013): «Nor indeed can a man of experience condemn even longer seasons of religious retirement, so they do not imply any neglect of the worldly employ wherein the providence of God has placed us. 2. Yet such retirement must not swallow up all our time;» Reason: Stepping away for rest with God daily, even longer retreats, is right, provided we do not abandon our calling.
2. #89 The More Excellent Way (wesley-089-c0041): «But we cannot be always intent upon business: Both our bodies and minds require some relaxation. We need intervals of diversion from business.» Reason: Body and mind need relaxation; constant work is not expected of a Christian.
3. #79 On Dissipation (wesley-079-c0019): «But it equally belongs to the serious fool who forgets God by a close attention to any worldly employment, suppose it were of the most elegant or the most important kind.» Reason: Warns that absorption in work, however important, can separate a person from God; names the spiritual danger of work consuming life.

column8: #89 The More Excellent Way, wesley-089-c0022 (proposed): What if you were to follow the advice given by that great and good man, Mr. Law, on this subject? Consider both your outward and inward state, and vary your prayers accordingly. For instance: Suppose your outward state is prosperous; suppose you are in a state of health, ease, and plenty, having your lot cast among kind relations, good neighbours, and agreeable friends, that love you and you them; then your outward state manifestly calls for praise and thanksgiving to God. On the other hand, if you are in a state of adversity; if God has laid trouble upon your loins; if you are in poverty, in want, in outward distress; «if you are in any imminent danger; if you are in pain and sickness; then you are clearly called to pour out your soul before God in such prayer as is suited to your circumstances.» Reason: Tells the person facing sickness or danger exactly what to do: pour out your soul to God in prayer fitted to your situation.
column9:
1. #98 On Visiting the Sick (wesley-098-c0026): «Does any thing then befall you without his knowledge, -- or without his designing it for your good? He knows all you suffer; he knows all your pains; he sees all your wants. He sees not only your affliction in general, but every particular circumstance of it.» Reason: Counsel for the sick: nothing befalls you without God knowing; he sees every pain and detail of your affliction.
2. #28 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 8 (wesley-028-c0066): «He shall remember thee when thou liest sick upon thy bed; when vain is the help of man. When all the things of earth can give no support, he will "make all thy bed in thy sickness."» Reason: Promise that God remembers and sustains the sick when human help is vain.
3. #82 On Temptation (wesley-082-c0045): «He removes the trouble, or sickness, or pain; and it is as though it never had been: At other times he does not make any outward change; outward trouble, or pain, or sickness continues; but the consolations of the Holy One so increase, as to over-balance them all;» Reason: When his children cry to him in sickness, God either removes it or gives consolation outweighing it; encouragement to pray.
4. #29 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 9 (wesley-029-c0076): «"Let the morrow," therefore, "take thought for the things of itself;" that is, when the morrow comes, then think of it. Live thou to-day. Be it thy earnest care to improve the present hour. This is your own; and it is your all. The past is as nothing, as though it had never been. The future is nothing to you.» Reason: Direct counsel against dread of what is coming: live today and leave tomorrow to God; fits anxious waiting.

column8: #94 On Family Religion, wesley-094-c0038 (proposed): And suppose, after you have done this, after you have taught you children from their early infancy, in the plainest manner you could, omitting no opportunity, and persevering therein, you did not presently see any fruit of your labour, «you must not conclude that there will be none. Possibly the "bread" which you have "cast upon the waters" may be "found after many days." The seed which has long remained in the ground may, at length, spring up into a plentiful harvest. Especially if you do not restrain prayer before God, if you continue instant herein with all supplication.» Meantime, whatever the effect of this be upon others, your reward is with the Most High. Reason: Tells a parent not seeing fruit with a child not to conclude there will be none, and to keep praying.

column8: #49 The Cure of Evil-speaking, wesley-049-c0013 (proposed): I. 1. «First, "If thy brother shall sin against thee, go and tell him of his fault, between thee and him alone."» The most literal way of following this first rule, where it is practicable, is the best: Therefore, if thou seest with thine own eyes a brother, a fellow Christian, commit undeniable sin, or hearest it with thine own ears, so that it is impossible for thee to doubt the fact, then thy part is plain: Take the very first opportunity of going to him; and, if thou canst have access, "tell him of his fault between thee and him alone." Indeed, great care is to be taken that this is done in a right spirit, and in a right manner. Reason: Wesley says not simply to let it go: go to the person privately, at the first opportunity, and tell them.
column9:
1. #83 On Patience (wesley-083-c0007): «patience of injuries; particularly affronts, reproach, or unjust censure? This teaches not to return evil for evil, or railing for railing; but contrariwise blessing.» Reason: Patience under unjust censure means not returning evil for evil; addresses how to bear being wronged by false report.
2. #26 Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 6 (wesley-026-c0072): «if any malice or bitterness, if any taint of unkindness or anger remains, if we do not clearly, fully, and from the heart, forgive all men their trespasses» Reason: Calls for forgiving from the heart, with no bitterness left; speaks to whether to let the wrong go.
3. #38 A Caution against Bigotry (wesley-038-c0072): «Rather labour, and watch, and pray the more, to confirm your love toward him. If he speak all manner of evil of you, speak all manner of good (that is true) of him.» Reason: If someone speaks evil of you, do not retaliate; speak truthful good of them and pray to keep loving.
